name: Emirati Pidgin Arabic
confidence_why: None of the ten works consulted describes word stress in Gulf or Emirati Pidgin Arabic; the only first-hand remark, in Altakhaineh, Al-Namer and Alnamer 2022, is an incidental observation that stress moves to the first syllable when Emirati Arabic geminates are lost (two nouns, judged by ten native listeners), which hints at initial stress but does not describe the system, so no placement or type can be stated with any confidence.
catalog_citation: Altakhaineh, Abdel Rahman Mitib, Abdul-Salam Al-Namer & Sulafah Alnamer. 2022. Degemination in Emirati Pidgin Arabic: A sociolinguistic perspective. Languages 7(1): 8, 13 pp. MDPI, open access (CC BY). doi:10.3390/languages7010008
catalog_locator: Sec. 4 'Results and Discussion', p. 8, paragraph after Table 4 and Table 5; background sec. 2.1.3 'Geminates in Arabic', p. 3; endnote 2, p. 12; naming-test items sec. 3.2.1 Table 2, p. 6.
catalog_quote: We also found during both the naming test and in the recorded conversation, a shift in syllable stress occurred from a penultimate or final syllable to the first one [i.e., leftward stress shift] in EPA. This unexpected shift was further checked by having 10 native EA speakers to listen to the respective excerpts and to judge the position of stress as well as whether the consonant is short or long. Table 5 below illustrates this concomitant shift. Table 5. The shift of the stress into the first syllable in the case of degemination. EA [Sa"GGaala] ‘maid’ EPA ["SaGaala]; EA [xa"jjaatQ] ‘tailor’ EPA ["xajaat] (sec. 4, p. 8 of 13) ... Note also that syllables with geminated phonemes tend to attract word stress, especially in the medial position2 . Degemination therefore also has an impact on word stress patterns. This feature was also given attention to in our study. (sec. 2.1.3, p. 3 of 13) ... [note 2, p. 12 of 13] It is worth pointing out that a syllable ending with a geminated consonant works as a long one as far as prosodic stress patterns are regarded, which means that it does actually carry word stress when it is the last prosodically long syllable in the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In Emirati Pidgin Arabic, words whose Emirati Arabic source carries stress on a (penultimate or final) syllable closed by a geminate lose the geminate and are pronounced with stress on the first syllable instead (leftward shift to initial). This is an observation restricted to degeminated nouns in a 10-item naming test plus conversation; the paper gives no general rule for GPA word stress, and no other opened description of GPA says anything about stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the shift is described as 'unexpected' and tied to degemination (sec. 2.1: 'Degemination therefore also has an impact on word stress patterns'). Some speakers retain geminates (40 of 300 tokens), for which no stress placement is reported.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms (picture-naming) and the same words in recorded conversation; word-level stress judged perceptually by 10 native Emirati Arabic listeners. Variety: GPA as spoken in Al Ain, UAE ('Emirati Pidgin Arabic'), speakers with L1 Malayalam, Hindi/Urdu, Pashto, Tagalog.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress remark found (Altakhaineh, Al-Namer & Alnamer 2022) concerns 'Emirati Pidgin Arabic' (GPA of blue-collar workers in Al Ain, UAE), a regional variety subsumed under pidg1248 (no separate glottocode). Other opened descriptions cover GPA in Buraimi/Oman (Naess 2008), Riyadh/Saudi Arabia (Almoaily 2013), Kuwait (Salem 2013) and multi-country data (Avram 2014, 2017, 2020); none of these says anything about word stress.
